items.title: Hello, World!
items.content:
## Hello, World!

C is a compiled language: a toolchain turns your source code into a machine-executable program before it runs. The classic first program is:

```c
#include <stdio.h>

int main(void) {
    printf("Hello, World!\n");
    return 0;
}
```

### How compilation works

You write source code in a `.c` file, then a compiler (GCC/Clang) translates it into machine code and links it into an executable. On Linux:

```bash
gcc hello.c -o hello
./hello
```

### The anatomy of a C program

- `#include <stdio.h>` pulls in the Standard Input/Output header so you can use `printf`.
- `int main(void)` is the entry point — the OS calls it when your program starts.
- `printf` writes text to standard output. `\n` is the newline character.
- `return 0;` signals success to the operating system.

### Comments

```c
// Single-line comment
/* Multi-line
   comment */
```

### Escape sequences

| Sequence | Meaning      |
|----------|--------------|
| `\n`     | Newline      |
| `\t`     | Tab          |
| `\\`    | Backslash    |
| `\"`     | Double quote |

---

**Next up:** variables and data types — how C stores values.

items.title: Variables and Data Types
items.content:
## Variables and Data Types

A **variable** is a named block of memory. Unlike Python, C requires you to declare a variable's type so the compiler knows how much memory to reserve:

```c
int age = 21;
double pi = 3.14;
char letter = 'A';
```

### Core types

| Type     | Size (typical) | Values                                  |
|----------|----------------|-----------------------------------------|
| `int`    | 4 bytes        | Whole numbers (e.g. `42`, `-7`)         |
| `double` | 8 bytes        | Floating point (e.g. `3.14159`)         |
| `float`  | 4 bytes        | Floating point, less precision          |
| `char`   | 1 byte         | A single character (`'A'`)              |
| `_Bool`  | 1 byte         | `0` or `1` (with `<stdbool.h>`: `true`) |

### Declaring and assigning

```c
int x;            // declaration (garbage until assigned)
x = 10;           // assignment
int y = 20;       // declaration + initialisation
```

### Integer types

`int`, `short`, `long`, `long long`, with optional `unsigned` to forbid negatives:

```c
unsigned int count = 100;
long long big = 9000000000LL;
```

### Format specifiers for printf

| Specifier | Type            |
|-----------|-----------------|
| `%d`      | `int`           |
| `%f`      | `double`/`float`|
| `%c`      | `char`          |
| `%s`      | string          |
| `%lu`     | `unsigned long` |

```c
printf("age: %d, pi: %.2f, letter: %c\n", age, pi, letter);
```

### sizeof

`sizeof` tells you the byte size of a type on your machine:

```c
printf("%zu\n", sizeof(int));   // usually 4
```

---

**Next up:** constants and basic input/output.

items.title: Constants and Basic Input/Output
Operators and Type Conversion
items.content:
## Operators and Type Conversion

### Arithmetic operators

| Operator | Meaning         |
|----------|-----------------|
| `+`      | Addition        |
| `-`      | Subtraction     |
| `*`      | Multiplication  |
| `/`      | Division        |
| `%`      | Remainder       |

Integer division truncates the fraction:

```c
printf("%d\n", 7 / 2);   // 3  (not 3.5)
printf("%d\n", 7 % 2);   // 1
```

To get true division, make at least one operand a `double`:

```c
printf("%f\n", 7.0 / 2); // 3.500000
```

### Increment and decrement

```c
int n = 5;
n++;        // n == 6  (post-increment)
++n;        // n == 7  (pre-increment)
```

`n++` evaluates to the old value; `++n` evaluates to the new value:

```c
int a = 5;
int b = a++;   // b == 5, a == 6
int c = ++a;   // a == 7, c == 7
```

### Assignment shortcuts

```c
x += 5;   // x = x + 5
x -= 2;   // x = x - 2
x *= 3;   // x = x * 3
x /= 4;   // x = x / 4
```

### Type conversion

**Implicit** conversion happens when types mix — `int` widens to `double`:

```c
int i = 3;
double d = 2.5;
double result = i * d;   // 7.5
```

**Explicit** conversion (casting) forces a type:

```c
int total = 7, count = 2;
double avg = (double)total / count;   // 3.5, not 3
```

### Relational operators

`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`, `<=`, `>=` produce an `int` that is `1` (true) or `0` (false).

---

**Next up:** exercises on variables, I/O, and arithmetic.

items.title: Functions: Declaration, Definition & Return
Return Values and Passing Data
Pointers: Addresses and Dereferencing
items.content:
## Pointers: Addresses and Dereferencing

A **pointer** is a variable that stores a memory address.

### The two operators

- `&` (address-of) — gives the address of a variable.
- `*` (dereference) — follows a pointer to the value it points to.

```c
int n = 42;
int *p = &n;      // p stores the address of n
printf("%p\n", (void*)p);   // the address
printf("%d\n", *p);         // 42  (the value at that address)
```

### Declaring pointers

```c
int *p;          // pointer to int
double *q;       // pointer to double
char *s;         // pointer to char
```

The `*` binds to the variable name, so `int *p, *q;` declares two pointers; `int *p, q;` declares one pointer and one plain `int`.

### Modifying through a pointer

```c
*p = 99;         // writes 99 into the memory p points to
printf("%d\n", n);   // 99
```

### Null pointers

A pointer should be set to `NULL` (or `0`) when it points to nothing meaningful:

```c
int *p = NULL;
if (p != NULL) {
    printf("%d\n", *p);   // safe only if p is valid
}
```

Dereferencing a null pointer is a segmentation fault.

### Why pointers matter

- Let functions modify caller variables (pass-by-reference).
- Enable dynamic memory allocation.
- Make arrays and strings work efficiently.
- Let data structures like linked lists exist.

---

**Next up:** pointer arithmetic and arrays.

items.title: Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays
items.content:
## Pointer Arithmetic and Arrays

An array's name is a pointer to its first element.

```c
int arr[4] = {10, 20, 30, 40};
int *p = arr;          // points to arr[0]
printf("%d\n", *p);    // 10
```

### Pointer arithmetic

Adding `k` to a pointer moves it `k * sizeof(element)` bytes forward:

```c
printf("%d\n", *(p + 1));   // 20
printf("%d\n", *(p + 3));   // 40
```

`p + 1` advances to the next element, not the next byte — the compiler scales by element size.

### Array notation is pointer notation

```c
arr[2] == *(arr + 2)     // always true
p[2] == *(p + 2)         // true too
```

### Iterating with a pointer

```c
for (int *q = arr; q < arr + 4; q++) {
    printf("%d ", *q);   // 10 20 30 40
}
```

### Strings and pointer arithmetic

C strings are `char` arrays terminated by a null byte:

```c
char *s = "hello";
while (*s != '\0') {
    putchar(*s);
    s++;                 // advance to next character
}
```

### Pointer to pointer

`char **argv` (used in `main(int argc, char **argv)`) is an array of string pointers.

items.title: Arrays: Declaration, Initialisation & Traversal
items.content:
## Arrays: Declaration, Initialisation & Traversal

An array stores a fixed-size sequence of elements of one type.

### Declaration

```c
int scores[5];              // 5 ints, uninitialised
int values[3] = {10, 20};   // {10, 20, 0}  — missing values zero-filled
double temps[4] = {0};      // all zeros
```

### Indexing

Indexes start at `0`. The last valid index is `size - 1`.

```c
scores[0] = 95;
printf("%d\n", scores[0]);
```

### Traversal

```c
for (int i = 0; i < 5; i++) {
    printf("%d ", scores[i]);
}
```

### Array size

```c
int arr[] = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5};
int n = sizeof(arr) / sizeof(arr[0]);   // 5
```

### Out-of-bounds danger

C does **not** check array bounds. `arr[10]` reads/writes whatever memory is there — a common source of bugs and security holes. Stay within bounds.

### Passing arrays to functions

The array decays to a pointer; a size parameter is required:

```c
void print_array(int arr[], int n) {
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) printf("%d ", arr[i]);
}
```

### Two-dimensional arrays

```c
int grid[2][3] = {{1, 2, 3}, {4, 5, 6}};
printf("%d\n", grid[1][2]);   // 6
```

---

**Next up:** strings — arrays of characters with a null terminator.

items.title: Strings: char Arrays and <string.h>
items.content:
## Strings: char Arrays and <string.h>

A C string is a `char` array ending in a null byte `'\0'`.

### String literals and arrays

```c
char greeting[] = "hi";          // {'h', 'i', '\0'}  — size 3
char *name = "Ada";              // pointer to read-only literal
char buffer[100];                // mutable buffer, uninitialised
```

### Null terminator

Every C string must end in `'\0'`. Functions like `printf("%s", ...)` keep reading until they hit it.

### Reading strings

```c
char line[100];
fgets(line, sizeof(line), stdin);      // safe, keeps newline
scanf("%99s", line);                   // reads one word, stops at space
```

### Common <string.h> functions

| Function      | Purpose                          |
|---------------|----------------------------------|
| `strlen(s)`   | Length (excludes `\0`)          |
| `strcpy(d,s)` | Copy `s` into `d`               |
| `strcmp(a,b)` | Compare: `<0`, `0`, `>0`        |
| `strcat(d,s)` | Append `s` to `d`               |
| `strchr(s,c)` | Find first `c` in `s`            |
| `strncpy`     | Copy at most n chars (safer)     |

```c
#include <string.h>

char src[] = "hello";
char dst[20];
strcpy(dst, src);
printf("%zu %d\n", strlen(dst), strcmp(dst, "world"));
```

### Iterating characters

```c
for (int i = 0; s[i] != '\0'; i++) {
    putchar(s[i]);
}
```

### String to number

```c
#include <stdlib.h>
int n = atoi("42");          // 42
double d = atof("3.14");     // 3.14
```

---

items.title: Dynamic Memory Allocation
items.content:
## Dynamic Memory Allocation

`malloc` and `free` let you allocate memory at runtime from the heap, for sizes unknown at compile time.

### malloc

```c
#include <stdlib.h>

int n = 10;
int *arr = malloc(n * sizeof(int));
if (arr == NULL) {          // always check!
    fprintf(stderr, "allocation failed\n");
    return 1;
}
```

### Using dynamic arrays

```c
for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) arr[i] = i * i;
```

### free

Return memory to the heap when done:

```c
free(arr);                  // after free, do not use arr again
```

Dangling pointers (using memory after `free`) and memory leaks (never calling `free`) are two classic C bugs.

### calloc and realloc

```c
int *zeroed = calloc(n, sizeof(int));      // zero-initialised
arr = realloc(arr, (n * 2) * sizeof(int)); // resize, preserving contents
```

### Lifetime summary

| Region  | Allocated        | Freed                |
|---------|------------------|----------------------|
| Stack   | function entry   | function exit        |
| Heap    | `malloc`/`calloc`| `free` (your job)    |
| Static  | program start    | program end          |

### Copying dynamic strings

```c
char *copy = malloc(strlen(src) + 1);      // +1 for '\0'
if (copy) strcpy(copy, src);
```

---

**Next up:** file input/output.

items.title: File Input and Output
The Preprocessor and Macros
items.content:
## The Preprocessor and Macros

The preprocessor runs before compilation and transforms the source text.

### #include

Textually inserts the contents of another file:

```c
#include <stdio.h>    // system headers
#include "myheader.h" // local headers
```

### #define macros

```c
#define PI 3.14159
#define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
```

Always parenthesise macro parameters to avoid precedence bugs:

```c
#define BAD(x) x * x
BAD(a + b)          // a + b * a + b  → WRONG
#define GOOD(x) ((x) * (x))
GOOD(a + b)         // ((a + b) * (a + b)) → correct
```

### Conditional compilation

```c
#ifdef DEBUG
    printf("debug mode\n");
#endif

#if defined(WIN32)
    // windows code
#else
    // other platforms
#endif
```

### #ifndef guards

Header files use include guards to prevent double inclusion:

```c
#ifndef MYHEADER_H
#define MYHEADER_H
/* declarations */
#endif
```

### #pragma once

A modern alternative to guards supported by most compilers:

```c
#pragma once
```

### Operators

```c
#define STR(x) #x          // # stringifies: STR(hi) → "hi"
#define JOIN(a,b) a##b     // ## concatenates tokens
```

---

**Next up:** header files and program organisation.
